posts.title: The Anatomy of a Monday Blind Tasting
posts.excerpt: Every Monday morning in Bordeaux, twelve hospitality professionals sit down at our oak table to taste six unlabelled wines and translate sensory instinct into precise service language.
posts.content:
At ten o'clock every Monday morning, the school room at 6 cour des Tonneliers in Bordeaux grows quiet. Twelve glasses sit in front of twelve servers, bartenders, and floor managers around the long light oak table. The bottles have been stripped of their capsules and wrapped in plain cloth, hiding every clue of grape variety, vintage, producer, and regional appellation. Morning window light illuminates the liquid, revealing hues ranging from pale green-tinted straw to deep, translucent garnet. For people who spend their evenings pouring wine under dim restaurant lights, this moment of morning stillness offers something rare: the chance to evaluate wine purely on structural evidence.

Hélène Marchetti, who founded Budou Academy in 2014 after eighteen years as a head sommelier, sits at the head of the table. Her instruction is simple and consistent: taste it, then name it. In the dining room, servers frequently rely on memorized producer stories, vintage prestige, or colorful tasting notes borrowed from distributor sheets. But when faced with an unlabelled glass, those marketing crutches disappear immediately. The only facts that matter are the ones physically present in the mouth. Is the acid tart or soft? Where does the tannin grip along the gums? Does the warmth on the finish indicate high alcohol, or is the palate balanced by concentrated fruit weight?

Blind tasting at Budou Academy is not an academic parlor trick or a high-stakes exam ritual. It is a daily working discipline designed specifically for people who work service floors. When a guest asks a server why a particular bottle tastes lean, crisp, or brooding, the server cannot offer vague generalities. They must understand how climate, grape variety, and cellar choices produce distinct structural markers. In our Monday morning flight of six wines, students evaluate acid levels, phenolic bitterness, oak influence, and fruit profiles step by step. They learn to eliminate possibilities systematically, mapping sensory signals directly to European wine laws, soil types, and regional traditions.

By noon, the table has worked through the entire flight. Discussion is lively and honest. A bartender from Turin debates skin contact duration with a bistro waiter from Lyon, while our service floor lead, Tomás Ferreira, guides their observations toward practical table vocabulary. There are no penalties for missing a grape variety or confusing adjacent sub-appellations. What matters is the ability to articulate structural balance and explain why the wine behaves as it does. When the group breaks for staff lunch at 13:00 to pair these very bottles against seasonal dishes, the morning's sensory notes immediately prove their worth in practice.

This weekly routine forms the heartbeat of our curriculum across all programmes, from the Service Floor Certificate to the Cellar & Trade Diploma. By repeating this sensory exercise every Monday across a term, our twelve students build a calm way of speaking that they can use on evening shifts. When service resumes on Tuesday night, they return to their dining rooms able to describe what is in the glass, and to say why it tastes like that.
